planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; give it shelter from harsh winter wind at the colder edge of its range.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, allowing room for its eventual wide, arching spread. Delavay tea olive is a Chinese species prized for its small, dark, glossy leaves and its uncommonly heavy spring floral display — dense clusters of small, pure white, jasmine-scented flowers smother the branches for several weeks, a much showier single bloom event than the scattered, repeat-blooming flushes typical of the more familiar sweet olive (O. fragrans). Its fine, dense texture and naturally graceful, mounding habit make it useful as an informal hedge, espalier, or foundation shrub, and it takes shearing well immediately after flowering if a tighter form is wanted. It is one of the more cold-hardy fragrant osmanthus species and is a parent of the popular hybrid O. x burkwoodii.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; site where its large, bold leaves have room to develop into a substantial screen.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese holly osmanthus is the boldest-leaved of the commonly grown fragrant osmanthus species, with long, leathery, dark-green leaves edged in stiff spiny teeth that look strikingly holly-like on a much larger, coarser scale than O. heterophyllus. Clusters of small, creamy-white flowers appear tucked along the stems in autumn, releasing the same sweet, carrying fragrance the genus is known for, though the flowers themselves are less conspicuous than the dramatic foliage. Its dense, upright growth and imposing texture make it an excellent large-scale screen, background shrub, or small evergreen tree with age, and it tolerates heavier shade than most other osmanthus while remaining relatively low-maintenance once established.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
